items.title: Vercel ships Virtual Models on AI Gateway — one ID you can re-point at a different model without a redeploy
items.summary: A virtual model (e.g. vmc/coding-agent) is a named alias over a real model plus its settings — fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, provider sort, tags — managed centrally in AI Gateway instead of hardcoded in app or agent code. Point an AI SDK call or a coding agent at the ID, and editing the alias changes what model every caller hits within a few minutes, no code change or redeploy. Settings are sticky across a swap, but provider-specific options stop applying once you point the alias at a different provider. No markup or platform fee on inference, including BYOK.
items.why: This moves 'which model does my coding agent use' out of code and into a config you can flip centrally — useful the next time a cheaper or better model shows up and you don't want to hunt down every hardcoded model string.
items.action: Create one virtual model for a single task, point one AI SDK call or your coding agent's model picker at the vmc/ ID, then test a provider swap on a candidate alias before editing the one in production.

eval.reason: A genuine new capability (named, centrally-managed model alias with sticky settings and fallbacks), not a rename of existing routing; not a duplicate of any prior brief.
Fresh fetch confirmed the article at this exact URL, dated Oct 28 2026, with all cited CLI/code examples present verbatim.

Cross-checked against the article: routing itself is not new (AI Gateway already did that), the new part is the named alias bundling model+settings; provider-specific settings not carrying over to a different provider is stated explicitly, not an inference.
Genuinely searched Vercel's own blog and a web search for a first-party demo video; none found as of this run.
Directly actionable for anyone running coding agents against multiple model providers; real config pattern, not marketing.

items.title: Matt Pocock's one-line fix for Codex subagents silently inheriting the parent's full context
items.summary: Some Codex models fork the parent conversation when they spawn a subagent, so it gets the parent's whole context window instead of a clean one scoped to its own brief — quietly defeating the point of a subagent for skills like code review or implement-spec. The fix (merged PR #1341, mattpocock/skills) is eight one-sentence edits telling every subagent-dispatching skill to explicitly ask for a fresh context window, plus a matching rule in the repo's own standards.
items.why: If you're using Codex (not just Claude Code) with any skill that spawns subagents, your subagent may be silently seeing your entire parent conversation instead of just its brief — check whether your own skills say so explicitly.
items.action: Grep your own skills/prompts for anywhere you dispatch a subagent and check it explicitly asks for a fresh context window — Codex won't assume that for you the way Claude Code's default does.

eval.reason: A real, specific fix for a concrete harness behavior bug (Codex forking context on subagent spawn), not a rehash or pure discourse; not a duplicate of any prior brief.

Fresh fetch of the LinkedIn post confirmed it live, ~20h old, 245 reactions / 26 comments; the embedded link resolves to the real GitHub PR #1341 (merged, mattpocock/skills), independently re-opened and confirmed.
PR description and diff confirmed: eight one-sentence edits across skill files plus a CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md repo-standard addition, matching the summary.

items.title: Arpit Bhayani: somewhere in your company is a vibe-coded production service nobody has actually read
items.summary: One person vibe-coded a service, watched it pass a few manual checks, and shipped it — they're the only one with any real feel for how it behaves, and most of the reasoning lived in an unsaved Claude session. His fixes: review generated code like any other code (if nobody on the team can explain it, it shouldn't ship), keep intent durable in code comments rather than a chat log, and make sure at least two people can operate and debug every production service.
items.why: A concrete, un-hyped checklist for the actual failure mode of fast AI-assisted shipping — not 'AI writes bad code' but 'nobody including the author can explain what's running.'
items.action: Pick one service on your team that one person vibe-coded solo and do the two-person debug test: can anyone besides the author explain why a specific non-obvious decision in it was made?

eval.reason: A genuine, specific practitioner take on a real failure mode, with concrete fixes, not a rehash; not a duplicate of any prior brief (confirmed distinct from this same author's earlier, differently-themed posts).
Fresh fetch confirmed the post live, 43 minutes old at time of check, 68 reactions / 5 comments, text matches exactly.

items.title: Karpathy built a personalized YouTube clone from Hacker News recommendations in ~2 hours with Claude Code — swyx's take: "effort levels are the tabs vs spaces of our time"
items.summary: Karpathy's own account: annoyed by YouTube's algorithm on a Friday night, he had Claude Opus 5.5 (Medium effort, via Claude Code) download and filter Hacker News comments from a public dataset, extract ~6,454 YouTube videos HN users have recommended since 2007, and wrap them in a YouTube-style UI at hackertube.org — his own manual work was getting an API key, booting a VPS, and buying a domain. swyx's reply: having a strong opinion on what effort level to default to is 'like the tabs vs spaces of our time.'
items.why: This is an actual working data point on what 'Medium effort, mostly hands-off' looks like for a real multi-hour build today, not just discourse about it.
items.action: If you haven't deliberately picked (and stuck with) a default effort level for your own agent work, this is a nudge to try one default for a week rather than re-deciding per task.

eval.reason: Real discourse anchored to a real, verifiable build (Karpathy's own blog post), not pure opinion; not a duplicate of any prior brief.

items.title: DeepSeek Harness's own writeup on 'Super-agent' design: a two-level Router/Worker architecture that beat single-session-plus-subagent by 40% on completion time
items.summary: Machine-translated from the team's original Chinese article. Their internal Super-agent runs continuously across IM and GitHub, not one session per task: a long-lived Router layer handles all human interaction and dispatch without executing work itself, while isolated Worker sessions run tasks concurrently — plus event-driven 'Triggers,' async full-duplex interaction, and a Watchdog session that monitors for stuck or drifting agents. In their own ablation (4 designs, 5 runs each, ~300 messages/run): Super-agent completed tasks in 12.4min (p50) / 15.7min (p95), versus 20.4min / 29.5min for a single-session-with-subagent-tool baseline using a neutral delegate-if-appropriate prompt — the baseline model didn't call a subagent in any of its 5 runs.
items.why: Real quantified evidence for a specific design decision — separate the router (dispatch-only) from workers (execution-only) — rather than trusting a single session's ad hoc judgment about when to delegate.
items.action: If your own agent setup leans on a single session's judgment about when to spin off a subagent, this ablation is a real data point for why that underperforms a structural router/worker split.

eval.reason: A genuine first-party architecture paper with real quantified ablation experiments (not a benchmark-only post or rehash); not a duplicate of any prior brief.
Fresh fetch confirmed the X Article live, verified account, published 5:07pm Nov 1 2026, 1.5M views / 333 comments / 1.7K reposts / 9.8K likes.
